summary: Mission Mars is a browser-based mission trainer that lets a child run a Mars colony for eleven sols. Five resources — water, oxygen, energy, food and materials — rise and fall in real time while the colony moves through 90-second days and nights. Twenty-five events, from dust storms and marsquakes to crew conflicts, appear in a Mission Log with four trade-off choices each, and ignoring one has its own consequence. Buildings have levels and build timers, research takes time, robots explore the surface and can break down, and a radio link to Houston answers 15 to 20 seconds late, the way real deep-space communication does. Every event, site and term is tagged with the open NASA source behind it: DONKI space weather, OSDR life sciences, Perseverance, Curiosity, InSight and SCaN. Losing opens a science debriefing instead of a "game over", so failure becomes a lesson. Three difficulty modes let younger and older players train at their own pace. Mars is the hook; systems thinking is the lesson.
details:
What it does and how it works. Mission Mars is a browser-based mission trainer where a child commands a Mars colony for eleven sols. The screen is a mission control center: a header with the mission clock and a day/night indicator, a COLONY RESOURCES panel with five live bars — water, oxygen, energy, food and materials — and a Mission Log that is the heart of the game. Every event appears there as a large Mars image, a timestamp, a short narrative and four big decision buttons. Time runs on a fixed cycle: 90 seconds of daylight and 90 seconds of night, three minutes per sol. Solar panels produce energy only in daylight, batteries carry the base through the night, and the crew keeps consuming water, oxygen and food the whole time. Twenty-five events are drawn at random and weighted toward pressure — 20% opportunities, 40% dilemmas, 40% crises — and every one of them has four choices with real trade-offs, hidden risks and a consequence if the player ignores the event for 60 seconds. Buildings have five levels and take time to build or upgrade. Ten research technologies reach three levels each and cost 30, 60 or 90 seconds per level. Robots with 100 hit points are built, sent to twenty real Martian sites such as Jezero Crater, Gale Crater, Utopia Planitia and Olympus Mons, and can break down and be repaired or lost. A radio link to Houston costs energy and answers 15 to 20 seconds late, the way deep-space communication really works. Winning means surviving to sol 11 and returning to Earth; losing opens a science debriefing that explains the cause, what was learned and one tip for the next flight.

Benefits and intended impact. The game teaches systems thinking: saving energy can starve oxygen, a fast trip can cost a robot, and a party raises morale but eats the food stores. Children practice reading trends, comparing costs and asking for help before an emergency grows — with no penalty for failing, because every loss is explained. It also makes open NASA data a story kids can touch, and it runs in any browser on a school computer or tablet with nothing to install.

Tools and languages. React 19 with TypeScript and TanStack Start, styled with Tailwind CSS v4. The whole simulation is one pure reducer in a single engine file, so every tab reads the same state and every rule can be unit-tested; 106 automated tests cover resource flow, death rules, research, robots, exploration, radio support and difficulty. Event art is generated imagery, and the project was built and iterated with Lovable.

What makes it creative. Instead of a quiz or a score, failure is rewritten as a debriefing; instead of instant answers, the radio reproduces real signal latency; instead of a "correct" option, each choice is only better or worse for the colony you actually have.

Factors considered. Difficulty for ages 7–12 without unfair punishment, honest sourcing of NASA data, screen simplicity and large touch targets, three difficulty modes, and no names, faces or voices of anyone under 18 anywhere in the project.

The file also has a ≈250-word version, the NASA data links for those fields, and a pre-paste checklist. I ran the tests to confirm the numbers quoted: 106 passing, 25 events, 20 sites, 10 researches, 8 buildings, 15–20 s radio delay.
